title: What CEOs Need to Know About Artificial General Intelligence
gist: BCG argues true AGI is unlikely near-term because LLM capability remains structurally 'jagged' (great at some tasks, weak at others) due to data exhaustion, RLVR's limits outside verifiable domains, lack of on-the-job learning, and compute/energy ceilings; CEOs should use a Pascal's-wager logic to plan for continued jaggedness and compete via 'token-based competition' rather than betting on AGI arriving.

insights.claim: AI's capability profile is 'jagged'—virtuoso at some skills, above average at others, below average at others still—and this unevenness, first identified in a 2023 study by BCG Institute researchers and academics, is the reason AI has not driven mass unemployment despite rapid model progress.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Investors should treat 'AI causes mass layoffs' narratives skeptically until jaggedness closes; job/wage disruption is gradual and uneven by task, not sector-wide.
insights.quote: it is a virtuoso at some skills, above average at others, and below average at others still
insights.locator: As AI models continue to make dramatic leaps

insights.claim: In software engineering—the most advanced applied-AI domain—AI has accelerated code generation and testing but still cannot own system-level judgment, architecture tradeoffs, stakeholder management, or outcome accountability; as a result, AI capabilities have become more jagged, humans have become more valuable, and software engineer employment continues to rise.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Contrary to fears of AI-driven engineer layoffs, hiring data in this sector is rising—an evidence point against near-term displacement theses for skilled knowledge work.
insights.quote: AI capabilities have become more jagged, humans have become more valuable, and employment of software engineers continues to rise.

insights.claim: The central open question for CEOs is whether AI's jaggedness is a temporary artifact that scaling laws (more compute and data) will close over the next decade, or a structural property of how LLMs acquire capability that would require a wholly different AI architecture—with an unknown timeline—to overcome.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: This scaling-vs-architecture debate is the single biggest swing factor for AGI timing—track it as the key variable rather than any single lab's launch announcement.
insights.locator: The key question is whether this jaggedness will persist

themes.theme: Scaling Skepticism in the Research Community

insights.claim: In a 2025 survey by the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI), 76% of respondents—mostly academics—agreed that scaling up current AI research approaches was 'unlikely' or 'very unlikely' to reach AGI, indicating the research community is markedly more skeptical of near-term AGI than some AI lab leaders.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
entities: Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence
insights.so_what: A large majority of the academic AI research community doubts pure scaling gets to AGI—useful counterweight when pricing AGI-timeline hype from commercial lab leaders.
insights.quote: 76% of respondents agreed that scaling up current AI research approaches was “unlikely” or “very unlikely” to reach AGI
insights.locator: Members of the AI research community skew even more conservatively

insights.claim: Early LLM progress came largely from scaling training data, but high-quality, readily accessible human-generated public text is finite, meaning pretraining-based gains have a natural ceiling—as OpenAI cofounder Ilya Sutskever put it, pretraining in its current form will end because there is only one internet.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Data exhaustion caps one of the two classic scaling levers (data), forcing labs toward synthetic data or RL-based methods with their own limits—watch for slowing pretraining gains as a leading indicator.
insights.quote: pretraining in its current form it will end, because there is only one internet

insights.claim: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)—rewarding AI for correctly repeated task completion—has driven large recent gains in math and code because outcomes there can be checked cheaply and reliably, but it is hard to extend to ambiguous, long-horizon knowledge work (e.g., 'is this the right product to launch' or a five-year investment strategy) where rewards are sparse, delayed, and contestable.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Expect continued fast AI gains in verifiable domains (code, math, quantitative tasks) but much slower progress in judgment-heavy knowledge work like strategy, product decisions, and long-horizon investing—segment AI-exposure assumptions accordingly.
insights.quote: Extending RLVR techniques to ambiguous, long-horizon work is hard because rewards are sparse, delayed, and contestable.

insights.claim: Today's LLMs generally do not update or 'learn on the job' while handling a task, unlike human employees who absorb an organization's history, culture, and tacit priorities through ongoing interactions—an unresolved constraint that limits AI's ability to perform roles where organizational context drives judgment.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Roles depending heavily on tacit, firm-specific knowledge (client relationships, internal politics, institutional memory) remain comparatively AI-resistant—a durable moat for incumbent staff versus AI substitution.
insights.quote: In other words, they do not “learn on the job.”

insights.claim: Even though more computing power reliably improves model performance, real physical limits on power generation, grid capacity, and semiconductor supply may make it impossible to allocate enough compute to a single training run capable of producing AGI.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Energy and chip supply constraints are a structural cap on AGI timelines, not just a cost issue—power/grid capacity and semiconductor availability become direct gating variables for frontier AI progress, relevant to energy and chip investment theses.
insights.locator: A Ceiling on Computing Power, Energy, or Hardware

themes.theme: Regulation as a Real-World AGI Constraint

insights.claim: On June 12, 2026, the US government ordered Anthropic to suspend all access to Mythos 5 and Fable 5 for foreign nationals citing cyberattack risk, and although the order was later reversed, the episode shows the government asserts authority to ban future AI models it deems too dangerous to release.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: National-security-driven model bans are now a live regulatory risk for frontier AI labs and their enterprise customers, not a hypothetical—factor government intervention risk into AI-vendor concentration decisions.

insights.claim: On June 25, 2026, the White House asked OpenAI to preemptively restrict release of GPT-5.6 (Sol/Terra/Luna) before its public launch—the first time the US government asked a company to restrict a model pre-release—leading OpenAI to initially limit its flagship model, Sol, to about 20 government-vetted partners.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Pre-release government gating of frontier model launches is now precedent, meaning commercial rollout timelines and access breadth for future flagship models are subject to political veto, not just technical readiness.
insights.quote: This marked the first time that the US government asked a company to restrict a model before releasing it.

insights.claim: On July 14, 2026, Demis Hassabis, co-founder and chair of Google DeepMind, published a manifesto proposing that the US create a standards body for frontier AI with power to approve new models prior to release to American users—an industry-originated push for pre-approval regulation.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: A top lab leader publicly proposing pre-approval regulation signals industry itself expects a licensing-style regime for frontier models—relevant to compliance cost and time-to-market assumptions for AI product roadmaps.
insights.quote: A Framework for Frontier AI and the Dawning of a New Age

insights.claim: On July 28, 2026, a statement called 'Pacing the Frontier' called on the US government to help build tools to deliberately slow frontier AI development, and more than 1,300 employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta signed it—showing significant internal industry appetite for deliberate deceleration.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Grassroots employee pressure at the largest AI labs for slower development is a signal that frontier AI pacing could shift for internal cultural/political reasons even absent formal law—watch for policy or internal-governance shifts at these labs.
insights.quote: More than 1,300 employees of OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and Meta have signed this letter.

insights.claim: Even if AGI is technically achieved, governments may gate access on national-security grounds—similar to how Boeing maintains separate divisions for commercial airlines versus defense, with its most cutting-edge aviation innovation reserved solely for government access—leaving a more jagged, capability-limited AI dominant in most commercial and consumer use.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: Even a technical AGI breakthrough may not translate into broad economic disruption if governments restrict distribution—commercial AI exposure may remain jagged-frontier-bound regardless of lab-level capability breakthroughs.
insights.locator: Of course, there are many examples of regulators

insights.claim: True AGI—virtuoso across all cognitive skills, rapidly absorbing all organizational tacit knowledge—would eliminate competitive advantage even for businesses with strong moats in physical goods or human-centric services, because the economic shock of widespread job loss among customers (and customers' customers) would be unpreparable-for regardless of strategy or technology investment.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: In a true-AGI scenario no strategic positioning protects a business—this caps the value of any AGI-hedging strategy work and argues against over-investing in preparation for that specific tail scenario.
insights.quote: No level of strategic planning or technology investment can help a CEO prepare for that scenario.

insights.claim: BCG applies Pascal's wager—the ~400-year-old logic that under irreducible uncertainty with vastly different outcomes and an unavoidable choice, one should embrace the value-maximizing choice—to conclude CEOs should prepare for a future where AI keeps growing in sophistication but retains capability limits, rather than planning around true AGI.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: A concrete decision rule for boards: allocate planning and capex toward the jagged-frontier scenario (align operating model to today's AI limits and prepare to adapt) rather than the all-or-nothing AGI scenario where no preparation helps.
insights.quote: the logical way to proceed is to identify and embrace the value-maximizing choice
insights.locator: A French mathematician named Blaise Pascal

insights.claim: The BCG Institute frames the durable competitive-advantage source in a persistently jagged-AI world as 'token-based competition'—since all companies will have access to the same powerful AI, differentiation will come from change management, skills development, incentive setting, and culture in figuring out how to best augment human teams with AI.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/greg-emerson
insights.so_what: As AI model access commoditizes, investors should value companies on execution capability (change management, incentive design, culture) rather than on AI access or model quality alone—that's where sustainable moats will actually form.
insights.quote: The BCG Institute describes this as “token-based competition.”
